topic.en: What the text is about: why household appliances stopped being repaired — the price of the machine, the price of an hour, parts, electronics and new rules.
topic.kk: Мәтін не туралы: тұрмыстық техниканы неге жөндемейтін болды — машинаның бағасы, шебердің сағаты, қосалқы бөлшек, электроника және жаңа ережелер.
topic.ru: О чём текст: почему бытовую технику перестали чинить — цена машины, цена часа мастера, запчасти, электроника и новые правила.

paragraphs.text: A washing machine bought in 1970 was expected to last twenty years and to be mended when it failed; the same machine today is expected to last seven, and when it fails it is usually replaced. The change is often explained by a single word, obsolescence, and the word does more harm than good, because it suggests a plan where there is mostly a set of separate decisions that each made sense to whoever made them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Start with the price of the machine. In real terms, household appliances cost between a third and a half of what they did two generations ago, which is an enormous gain for households that could not previously afford them. The saving was achieved by moulding rather than machining, by fewer and cheaper fasteners, by assembly designed for a robot, and by thinner steel. Every one of those choices makes a machine harder to open and less worth opening, and none of them was made in order to shorten its life.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Then consider the price of the repair. The cost of a visit is dominated by an hour of a trained person’s time plus travel, and labour has become steadily more expensive relative to goods. When the visit costs a third of a new machine before any part is fitted, the arithmetic decides itself, and it decides the same way even for a fault that takes ten minutes to fix. This is why repair survives best where labour is cheap relative to goods and disappears where it is not.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Parts are the part of the story where intent is easier to see. Manufacturers who publish exploded diagrams, sell components to anyone and keep them in stock for a decade make repair possible; those who supply only complete assemblies, restrict sales to authorised agents or stop production of spares after three years make it impossible whatever the repairer wants. Both business models exist in the same market, which is the clearest evidence that the outcome is a choice rather than a law of manufacturing.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Electronics changed the failure pattern rather than the failure rate. A mechanical timer failed gradually and audibly; a control board fails completely and silently, and diagnosis needs equipment that an independent workshop may not have. Where the board is unique to one model and is sold only as a unit, its price is frequently set at a level that makes replacing the appliance the rational choice. The board itself is rarely the expensive component; the pricing is a decision about the service business, not about the electronics.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Law has started to intervene, unevenly. Several jurisdictions now require that spare parts be available for a fixed number of years after a model is withdrawn, that some repairs be possible with ordinary tools, and that a repairability score be printed beside the price. Early evaluations of the score are mildly encouraging: it shifts purchasing towards the better-rated models and, more interestingly, appears to change what manufacturers design, since a low score is visible to buyers in a way that a design decision is not.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The repair trade itself has thinned, and it does not come back quickly. Independent workshops closed as volumes fell; the skills went with the people who had them, and the training routes closed behind them. Cities that now want a repair sector discover that it is not enough to create demand, because there is nobody to meet it for a few years, and that the work has shifted towards community repair sessions run by volunteers, which are excellent at small fixes and cannot absorb the work of a trade.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The honest summary is that mending is worth arguing for and that the argument is not mainly about virtue. A machine kept for fifteen years instead of seven halves its share of the materials and the emissions of manufacture, which no amount of recycling matches. But the reason mending stopped was cheapness, and the reason it can resume is that the relative prices are moving again: energy, metals and shipping have all risen, and a repair that made no sense in 2015 makes arithmetic sense now. That is a better foundation for the trade than any appeal to how things used to be.
paragraphs.label: H
